title: Never Skip a Batch: Dense Learning of Temporal GNNs via Adaptive Pseudo-Supervision

problem.claim: Temporal graph networks receive irregular and sparse supervision in real-world dynamic graphs because most minibatches contain few labeled events.

gap.claim: The lack of labels causes high-variance gradient updates and slow wall-clock convergence.

contributions.claim: Moving-Averaged Labels (MAL) assigns soft pseudo-targets from past supervised signals using a running label distribution, without changing the loss or model architecture.
The paper provides theoretical analysis that historical supervision aggregated into moving-average targets reduces stochastic gradient variance and supports faster convergence under mild assumptions.
MAL is designed to replace supervision gaps with informative signals independently of the temporal graph model and its message-passing or memory components.

author_reported_evidence.claim: On TGNv2 and DyRepv2, MAL reportedly boosts predictive performance.
MAL reportedly improves time-to-accuracy, reaching the top score on average 6(Õ) faster.

narrative_sequence.summary: Temporal graph networks encounter sparse labeled events in most minibatches.
Sparse supervision produces high-variance gradients and slower wall-clock convergence.
MAL supplies soft pseudo-targets from historical supervised signals without modifying the loss or architecture.
The authors argue that moving-average targets reduce stochastic gradient variance and accelerate convergence under mild assumptions.
Experiments on TGNv2 and DyRepv2 report improved predictive performance and faster time-to-accuracy on Temporal Graph Benchmark datasets.

source_observation.claim: Historical supervised signals are aggregated into moving-average pseudo-targets to fill supervision gaps.

interpretation.claim: When labeled events are sparse, soft targets derived from recent supervision may provide denser training signals without changing the model architecture.

application.claim: This pattern may apply to other minibatch learning settings with intermittent labels and costly convergence.

exception.claim: The reported convergence benefit is theoretically supported only under mild assumptions.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify the exact running-label update rule or pseudo-target weighting.
The exact datasets, evaluation metrics, and meaning of the reported 6(Õ) speedup are not provided.
The mild assumptions underlying the convergence analysis are not described.
